sources.entry: The tao of programming: a set of parables about programming.

summary.title: The Tao of Programming
summary.one_liner: A collection of short, humorous parables in the style of Taoist teaching that comment on software design, management, maintenance and programmer attitudes.
takeaways: The "Law of Least Astonishment": a program should respond to users in the way that least surprises them.
Design changes become too late once a program is in testing, and adding programmers to a project does not always shorten it.
Software that is not used rots, and even short programs eventually need maintenance.
Management and organizational dysfunction are satirized through stories about meetings, budgets and corporate memos.
Programming is compared to Taoist ideas of simplicity, harmony and non-striving.
summary.summary: This page is a copy of a set of short parables about programming, written in the style of Taoist teaching texts, with a Master Programmer, novices, managers and a Grand Master Turing as characters. Each parable is a brief anecdote or dialogue followed by a terse aphorism, and the pieces cover design, debugging, documentation, testing, management, corporate bureaucracy and the relationship between hardware, software and firmware. The text is presented as humour and commentary rather than instruction, and it contains no technical tutorial content. The page notes that it was copied from an earlier NASA-hosted version and had its formatting removed.
